L1.arrival: Use the Metroparks destination pin and park in the small visitor lot (Berea Falls Trailhead). Walk the short path to the wooden overlook deck.

Metroparks hours are 6 a.m.–11 p.m., but daylight matters more. Aim to be here before about 4:30 p.m. in winter.

chapters.title: The Envelope
chapters.intro: Claire Marsh’s message reaches your phone as the drinks arrive. Her aunt Helen drowned eleven days ago, and the police called it an accident. Claire doesn’t believe them. Helen mailed her an envelope the day she died. Claire wants two patient people to look at it before she takes it to anyone official.
chapters.outro: Helen’s first message is open, and so is her first destination. Finish your drinks — there’s no hurry. When you’re ready, drive to the falls.

chapters.title: Where the Stone Breaks
chapters.intro: Helen spent forty years reading rock. Whatever she meant you to understand, she meant you to understand it here, watching the river work.
chapters.outro: Helen went to meet someone the night she died. To prove what she found, you have to read the same stones she read — in town, where the quarries began.

chapters.title: Words in Stone
chapters.intro: Helen’s last notebook page has no date and no name. It has one paragraph in her handwriting, which wanders more than usual. Claire thought it was a poem. It isn’t.
chapters.outro: Now you know what Helen knew. Someone else knew it too. Find somewhere comfortable — a bench, a café, your car once you’ve left the lot — and open the last folder.

chapters.title: The Pit at Night
chapters.intro: Claire has requested the records she can legally get. They arrived this afternoon, and they are short. Everything in them is accurate.

blocks.x: Thank you for doing this. I don’t know who else to ask.

Aunt Helen was a geologist — forty years of rocks and quarries. Lately she was an outside reader for Halberd & Finch, the Cleveland auction house. They had her check a letter they’re selling: a letter John Baldwin supposedly wrote in 1849. Estimate $85,000.

Eleven days ago they found her in the water at the old Larkmoor pit, a flooded private quarry outside town. Thursday night. They say she slipped on a wet ledge. Helen never went near ledges at night. She used to lecture ME about it.
The same day, she mailed me an envelope: a copy of the letter, the paperwork, and pages from her notebook. Half of it is in some code of hers. Please read it. Tell me if I’m crazy.
— Claire

E02.title: The Promenade Letter (Lot 112)
E02.caption: Auction catalogue transcription of a letter dated 12 June 1849, signed “J. Baldwin.” The text and the letter are fictional.

blocks.x: Berea, 12th June 1849.
My dear Brother,
The Seminary trustees having given the Triangle to the people two summers past, to be kept forever a public promenade, our little town has a heart at last.
Our grindstones go out by every wagon, and the stone keeps faith with us.
The town pump at the south-east angle of the promenade draws a crowd each market morning.
On the Sabbath the brethren of the Congregational church gather beneath their meeting-house spire, a full hundred feet above the square.
And where the old pit lies, all is now nothing but a quiet, blue body of water, glimmering in the sunlight.
Yr. affectionate brother,
J. Baldwin
Lot 112. Paper is old — rag, right weight. Ink is right. The LOOK is right.
It’s the words.
If I’m right: V. loses $85,000. D. signed the catalogue. O. keeps asking about the house.
Writing the rest my way. My emails are being read — I’m sure of it.
SER IRSSRP FQ T IFR. SER QSLKR PRJRJARPQ. ARDFK WERPR SER PFVRP APRTHQ FS.
Key: the name that lost the toss. One word.

falls
A waterfall here isn’t water winning. It’s stone losing, in order. Put it in order and you’ll see how Lot 112 fails too: a hard, honest face over something soft.
Stand at the rail. Watch the lip. Ask what’s holding it up.

“The raging waters of Rocky River that formed the Berea Falls are a piece of glacial history. Post-glacial river water found its way along the Berea sandstone, seeping through fissures and cracks to the soft shale below. As the shale eroded, the sandstone on top was undermined and began to break off. Those breaks in turn became the Berea Falls.”

source.label: Cleveland Metroparks, Berea Falls Scenic Overlook (reviewed 2026-11-12)

E14.title: Reference: Ohio Historical Marker 16-18
E14.caption: Official text of the marker at the north end of Coe Lake Park (erected 1998).

blocks.x: Berea Sandstone Quarries / The “Big Quarry”
Side A

For more than ninety years, this area was the heart and soul of Berea’s sandstone quarries. In the early 1830s, John Baldwin discovered that the area’s sandstone deposits made superb grindstones and building stones. In the 1840s, thriving sandstone quarries developed and became Berea’s lifeblood. Searching for the “American Dream,” German, Irish, Italian, Hungarian, and Polish immigrants, among others, came here to work. The quarries eventually encompassed nearly 250 acres and consumed the fashionable houses of Berea’s “South Side” and the buildings of Baldwin University. The Cuyahoga County Court House, Ohio’s Capitol, and Canada’s parliament buildings are among many structures in North America and Europe constructed of Berea sandstone. Decreasing demand for sandstone and the Great Depression closed the last of Berea’s quarries in the mid-1930s.
Side B

The photograph looks north to the buildings on East Bridge Street, which constituted the northern boundary of Berea’s sandstone quarries around 1895. The photographer stood approximately where you are standing. “Gradually the water came, first a little pool, then it rose higher and higher, until at last the workmen gathered up their tools and left the water to fill to the brim this basin they had made in the earth, until that place formerly so full of busy sounds was nothing but a quiet, blue body of water, glimmering in the sunlight.” Anna M. Nokes, “The Big Quarry,” 1895 (Nokes was a Baldwin University student.)

source.label: Ohio History Connection, Remarkable Ohio, marker 16-18 (reviewed 2026-11-12)

E16.title: Reference: Ohio Historical Marker 82-18
E16.caption: Official text of the marker at the northwest corner of Seminary Street and Church Street. The plate itself carries the number transposed, as 18-82.

blocks.x: First Congregational United Church of Christ of Berea

Seven original members, who were staunch abolitionists, organized the First Congregational Church of Berea in the nearby Union School House on June 9, 1855. These members publicly articulated opposition to slavery and their desire for a church with full local autonomy. The church purchased this property and erected this sanctuary in 1869, the oldest still standing structure used as a church in Berea and the original Middleburg Township. It is constructed of locally manufactured brick with a foundation from the Berea sandstone quarries. The 100-foot spire was added in 1954 to celebrate its 100th anniversary since the founding of the church in 1855. The church joined the newly formed United Church of Christ in 1961. During its long history, the church has developed many programs to assist persons in need in the Berea area and developed collaborative ventures with other churches and civic groups.

source.label: Ohio History Connection, Remarkable Ohio, marker 82-18 (reviewed 2026-11-12)

blocks.x: The paper is genuinely old. The words are not. Whoever wrote the letter built it from modern historical markers. They copied the true details and got caught by two they couldn’t have known in 1849: a church that didn’t exist yet, under a spire added in 1954, and a student’s description of a flooded quarry from 1895.
Anyone selling the letter would want that kept quiet. Only one person could explain where the paper really came from.

hints: The key is in the clipping Helen pinned to the page. A coin decided between two names.
Berea won the toss. What was the other name?
The losing name was Tabor (as in Mount Tabor). Helen said one word, so try TABOR.

reveal.why: The clipping says Berea was chosen over “Tabor (Mount Tabor)” on a coin toss. Helen’s key is “the name that lost the toss. One word,” so the key is TABOR. Her alphabet is T A B O R followed by the unused letters C D E F G H I J K L M N P Q S U V W X Y Z. Each coded letter stands where its plain letter sits in the normal alphabet, so T→A, A→B, B→C, O→D, R→E, and so on. Decoded: “THE LETTER IS A LIE. THE STONE REMEMBERS. BEGIN WHERE THE RIVER BREAKS IT.”

P2.title: Where the river breaks it
P2.objective: Which of Helen’s pinned places does her message send you to?

near.02314cf74c22f9af6db76ce95b954121b9822988: Stone lies beneath it, but there’s no river.

Berea Falls: the river undermines the sandstone until it breaks off.

reveal.why: “Begin where the river breaks it” — “it” is the stone from the line before. Coe Lake and Wallace Lake are still, flooded quarries. The Triangle has no river. Only at Berea Falls does a river break stone: Metroparks describes the Rocky River wearing away the shale until the sandstone above breaks off.

P3.title: How the stone loses
P3.objective: Put Helen’s four cards in the order the falls actually formed.
P3.onSite: From the overlook deck, look at the falls: water sliding over a hard edge of rock and dropping below. Then sort the cards.

items.x: The unsupported sandstone cracks and breaks off — a falls is born.
River water seeps down through cracks in the hard sandstone.
With nothing beneath it, the sandstone ledge hangs out over empty space.
The soft shale below the sandstone wears away.

hints: The hard layer is on top and the soft one is below. Which one can the water attack first, and how does it get there?
Water has to get down to the soft layer before anything else can happen.
Seep through cracks → soft shale wears away → sandstone left hanging → sandstone breaks off.

reveal.answer: Seep → shale wears → ledge hangs → breaks off
reveal.why: The sandstone is the hard top layer, so the water can’t cut it head-on. It seeps through cracks to the soft shale below. As the shale wears away, the sandstone above loses its support and juts out. Eventually it breaks off, and the breaks make the falls. This is the Metroparks explanation. Helen’s point: a hard, honest face can fail because of what’s underneath it.

reveal.why: Side B of marker 16-18 quotes Anna M. Nokes’s 1895 essay “The Big Quarry.” Her passage ends “…nothing but a quiet, blue body of water, glimmering in the sunlight.” The Promenade Letter, dated 1849, ends with those same words. A letter can’t quote an essay written 46 years later. And in 1849 the quarries were booming, not flooded. Standing there, you can see why Helen wrote “where have I read this before?”

P6.title: Two summers past
P6.objective: Check each line of the Promenade Letter. Which lines are contradicted by the markers, and which aren’t?
P6.onSite: Walk one block north on Seminary Street to the marker at the corner of Church Street. Read it, and remember that the letter claims 1849.

items.x: “The Seminary trustees having given the Triangle to the people two summers past, to be kept forever a public promenade…”
“Our grindstones go out by every wagon…”
“The town pump at the south-east angle of the promenade…”
“…the Congregational church… their meeting-house spire, a full hundred feet above the square.”
“…nothing but a quiet, blue body of water, glimmering in the sunlight.”

hints: Judge every line against 1849. “Not contradicted” doesn’t mean proven; it means nothing on the markers rules it out.

The Triangle went to the people in 1847, which is two summers before 1849. Grindstones date to the 1830s and the quarries were thriving in the 1840s. The pump stood there until 1924, and its start date isn’t given. Now read the church marker’s dates.
Contradicted: the church (organized 1855; 100-foot spire added 1954) and the flooded quarry (Nokes, 1895). The other three aren’t contradicted.

reveal.answer: Contradicted: the church spire and the blue water
reveal.why: Two summers before 1849 is 1847, the year the Triangle was deeded as a public promenade, so that fits. Grindstones (1830s) and thriving 1840s quarries fit. The marker says the pump stood on the southeast angle until 1924 and gives no start date, so nothing rules it out. But the Congregational church wasn’t organized until June 9, 1855, and its 100-foot spire went up in 1954. The flooded quarry is described in words written in 1895. The forger copied the true details carefully and gave themselves away with the two they couldn’t have known.

reveal.why: Helen went to meet “the one person who knows where the paper truly came from.” Victor’s bill of sale says the estate details were “held by seller; not disclosed to buyer.” Victor never knew, and only Iris did. Iris also had the skill: as a conservator she handled real old paper and period ink, and her own note vouches that both are genuine, which they were. The words were the forgery, built from modern markers. Dana and Owen were too far away, and Victor didn’t know what Helen needed to ask.

ending.headline: Case closed: Iris Calloway
short: Claire took your findings to the county prosecutor the next morning: two impossible lines, a restored page and a bill of sale.

Iris had taken a blank sheet of genuine 1840s rag paper from a ruined ledger. She wrote the letter in period ink, copying phrases she had read on Berea’s historical markers. When Helen asked to see the estate trunk the letter supposedly came from, Iris chose the place: an old quarry, at night. Lot 112 has been withdrawn, and Helen’s death is being investigated again.

full.head: The forgery
full.x: The paper and ink were genuinely old, which is why the conservation note was honest and the letter looked right. The words were new. Three of the letter’s details are real Berea history copied from markers: the 1847 promenade deed, the grindstones and the town pump. Two are impossible in 1849. The Congregational church wasn’t organized until 1855, and its 100-foot spire dates from 1954. The “quiet, blue body of water” is Anna M. Nokes describing the flooded Big Quarry in 1895.

full.head: The meeting
full.x: Helen’s torn page shows she went to the Larkmoor pit to meet “the one person who knows where the paper truly came from.” She wasn’t there by accident.

full.head: Opportunity
full.x: The examiner’s window is 7:15–8:30 pm. Owen was in the air. Dana left Cleveland at 8:05 and couldn’t arrive before about 8:40. Victor and Iris both could have been there.

full.head: Knowledge
full.x: Victor bought the letter for $4,000 from Iris, and the estate details were withheld from him. He stood to lose $85,000, which made him look guilty, but he was the forger’s mark, not the forger. Only Iris knew where the paper came from, so only Iris was the person Helen went to meet.

full.head: Fact and fiction
full.x: Everything about the people and Lot 112 is invented. The marker texts, the coin toss and the geology of the falls are real, quoted from the Ohio History Connection, the City of Berea and Cleveland Metroparks.
